title: Meta's Wang Says Superintelligence Is Arriving, Stripe's AI Surge | OWITH Daily
description:
Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang says superintelligence is arriving, pointing to a claimed Riemann hypothesis proof made with Claude, while Stripe reports a fifty percent jump in new customer sign ups. Plus autopilot software for satellites, Cerebras's one thousand employee millionaires, a radiology staffing gap a decade after Hinton's prediction, and an AI aid finder for disaster survivors.

Good morning from OWITH.ai, the briefing that gives you only what's important to hear in AI and tech. It's Wednesday, November 25.

Today, Meta's AI chief says superintelligence is arriving, and Stripe offers rare hard numbers on how fast business is changing.

Our lead comes from Meta. Fortune reports that Alexandr Wang, who runs Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X over the weekend that superintelligence is arriving. He said models will soon be able to automate all AI research, and that it is hard to picture humanity keeping control of unconstrained recursive self improvement. He pointed to a claim by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's staff, to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with help from Claude. That proof still awaits expert review, and the one million dollar Clay prize remains unclaimed. After a backlash, Wang added that the path remains a choice and that leadership matters more than ever. When a lab leader talks this way, boards should expect regulators to listen.

Next, evidence from the payments business. Fortune reports that Stripe's new customer sign ups have risen fifty percent year over year, its largest jump on record. The median business in its twenty twenty six group of new customers is generating fifty percent more revenue than the median business from twenty twenty five at the same stage. In an August letter, cofounders Patrick and John Collison wrote that the world entered the Singularity on January first, and that Stripe operates on that basis. Fortune notes the figures do not show how much of the gain comes from AI. A McKinsey survey found about thirty seven percent of respondents saw AI lift earnings, mostly by small amounts. Finance chiefs should measure their own gains before buying the narrative.

Space is getting crowded, and one startup wants satellites to steer themselves. Fortune reports that BQP, a simulation company based in Syracuse, New York, is building what founder Abhishek Chopra calls autopilot for satellites. NASA estimates that orbital debris costs American satellites about fifty eight million dollars a year, and a single avoidance maneuver about one million dollars in fuel. BQP says its software can simulate every object in orbit in under thirty minutes, a job Chopra says takes current tools about forty days. In July it won a small research award from SpaceWERX, the Space Force's innovation arm, and IBM Ventures invested in September, bringing total funding to eight million dollars. Autonomy in orbit is becoming a defense budget line.

AI wealth is also spreading through the chip industry. Cerebras chief executive Andrew Feldman said on the Sourcery podcast with Molly O'Shea that the company has made more than one thousand employees millionaires. Fortune values Cerebras at about twenty one point seven billion dollars. Its May listing raised five point five five billion dollars at one hundred eighty five dollars a share. Feldman's advice to staff is to diversify, because holding nearly all your wealth in one stock is unwise even when the company is doing well. He warned that big swings in personal wealth, up and down, are really stressful. For employers, equity is now a retention tool and a wellbeing issue at once.

In twenty sixteen, Geoffrey Hinton said the world should stop training radiologists. A decade later, a Fortune commentary by Patrick O'Donnell of the nonprofit Ridgeline and Mike Jones of UCSF says the Bay Area has about two thousand nine hundred twenty radiologic technologists, roughly six hundred fewer than a labor market its size should have, according to Lightcast data. Over the past year, the region saw about one hire for every four job postings, and median pay is about one hundred forty two thousand dollars. The authors argue that AI has kept the job alive but may be removing the routine work beginners used to learn on. Workforce plans built on confident AI forecasts deserve a second look.

Finally, disaster recovery. Jonathon Nostrant, whose Los Angeles home survived the Palisades fire, cofounded AidFinder, a Miami startup that uses AI to match survivors with aid programs and prepare applications for them to review. Fortune reports it is still a pitch. It has no state customer yet, though Nostrant told Refresh Miami it is in talks with thirty states, including Florida. Former FEMA chief Craig Fugate has joined its board. The timing follows policy. According to Nostrant, FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton has told state emergency managers to prepare to handle more recovery work themselves. As Washington steps back, states become the buyers of public sector AI.

The thread today is that AI's promises are running ahead of the proof, from a math claim still under review to a staffing forecast that missed, and the people who check the details will decide what holds. That's it for today. Thanks for listening to OWITH.ai. See you tomorrow.
